title: Do Vision-Language Models Respect Contextual Integrity in Location Disclosure?
claim: Models can fail by withholding information that is safe to share or by revealing information that should stay private, depending on context.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right, two stacked example rows, ✗/✓ marks
description: A three-column diagram, read left to right, with two example rows. The left column, headed 'Image', shows a photo of a Las Vegas Eiffel Tower replica with a blurred face (top) and a crowded protest inside a government building (bottom). Curved arrows lead from each image to two blue rounded boxes under 'VLM Response'. Each box holds a model reply. Gray arrows link each reply to a colored label: red 'Under Disclosure' and 'Over Disclosure', and green 'Valid Disclosure' and 'Valid Refusal'. Black circles with ✗ or ✓ mark each label as wrong or right. On the right, purple 'Human Expectations' boxes explain the norm, either that revealing the location is fine or that it should not be revealed. The red/green coding draws the eye first.
caption: Vision Language Models (VLMs) often do not reflect human expectations of information disclosure about images provided in context. For instance, they may limit their helpfulness by under-disclosing location information, such as by failing to provide the exact location of an image of a distinctive landmark (top). Alternatively, VLMs may compromise user privacy by over-disclosing location information, such as by providing the exact location of a political protest (bottom). We introduce \dataset to evaluate the incidence of over- and under-disclosure of location information by VLMs. Faces are blurred for presentation to protect privacy.
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in image geolocation, a capability further sharpened by frontier multimodal large reasoning models (MLRMs). This poses a significant privacy risk, as these widely accessible models can be exploited to infer sensitive locations from casually shared photos, often at street-level precision, potentially surpassing the level of detail the sharer consented or intended to disclose. While recent work has proposed applying a blanket restriction on geolocation disclosure to combat this risk, these measures fail to distinguish valid geolocation uses from malicious behavior. Instead, VLMs should maintain contextual integrity by reasoning about elements within an image to determine the appropriate level of information disclosure, balancing privacy and utility. To evaluate how well models respect contextual integrity, we introduce VLM-GEOPRIVACY, a benchmark that challenges VLMs to interpret latent social norms and contextual cues in real-world images and determine the appropriate level of location disclosure. Our evaluation of 14 leading VLMs shows that, despite their ability to precisely geolocate images, the models are poorly aligned with human privacy expectations. They often over-disclose in sensitive contexts and are vulnerable to prompt-based attacks. Our results call for new design principles in multimodal systems to incorporate context-conditioned privacy reasoning.
